extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theory and public opinion; educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and analyzes the conditions, assumptions, and institutional remedies Lippmann describes as necessary for democratic government and public opinion to function. Focuses on what must be true about information, community size, security, and institutional design for democracy to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption of innate political wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Political science assumed the art of government to be a natural endowment — that political wisdom appears spontaneously in certain men or classes (kings, landholders, farmers, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann cites the shared major premise from Aristotle through early democratic theorists: debates differ only on which persons are 'born' or naturally fitted to govern. Examples: royalists asserting kings, Hamilton expecting landholders/merchants to dominate, Jefferson claiming farmers possess political faculties. This assumption underpins choices about who should rule and absolves theorists from specifying how rulers acquire worldly knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the world taken for granted
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding who is fit to govern, political thought historically took knowledge of the wider world as given and did not address how to bring reliable worldly knowledge to rulers or voters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann notes it was 'no part of political science' to work out how to inform the ruler; consequently theorists assumed voters/rulers acquired necessary facts 'as they took in their breath.' This omission creates a gap between the ideal of self-government and the practical problem of informing decision-makers about distant/complex matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of attention must be limited for spontaneous politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Spontaneous politics (where citizens judge public affairs directly) is only feasible in an environment confined to the direct and certain knowledge of the ruler or voter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Aristotle: if citizens must judge by merit they must know each other's characters — absent that, elections and laws go wrong. Lippmann argues that ancient and early modern theory presupposed a small, local sphere of affairs; when public affairs extend beyond that sphere, spontaneous self-government becomes unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for instruments (reporting, measurement, record) to extend judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing unseen, distant, and complex events into the field of public judgment requires inventions such as newspapers, press services, photography, quantitative measurement, and psychological analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann emphasizes that these are the 'key inventions' that make continuous reporting feasible. While often done poorly, they permit the unseen world to be reported, analyzed, and presented so that amateurs can make valuable choices — a radical change from previous political assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-contained community requirement for democratic functioning
rubrics_metrics.description: For democracy to work as originally conceived, the community must be simple, self-contained, and capable of being self-sufficient — conditions approximated by small rural townships and independent farmers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann discusses Jefferson's vision: farmers in isolated communities are the ideal democratic citizens because their daily experience matches the sphere of public affairs they govern. Where such insulation from external complexities is impossible, the democratic stereotype breaks down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omnicompetent citizen assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic theory often assumes that one citizen is as competent as another to manage public affairs within a simple, self-contained environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In townships, rotation in office and a jack-of-all-trades approach make this plausible. Lippmann warns the assumption fails when applied universally to complex, large-scale societies where specialized knowledge and sustained interest vary widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on stereotyped images and homogeneous codes of morals
rubrics_metrics.description: In self-contained communities public opinion forms from stereotyped images supplied by parents, teachers, church, local experience, and legal codes rather than from broad objective reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann argues that with limited media and experience, citizens' pictures of the outside world are unchallenged and standardized; the community 'takes its supply of information for granted,' making differences mostly logical applications of shared premises rather than grounded factual disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security and minimal disturbance as preconditions for democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy requires as little disturbance as possible; insecurity (surprises, novel external forces) forces decisions into the hands of a few and is therefore incompatible with spontaneous, mass-based democratic decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann contends democracies prefer peace and stability because rapid, novel crises demand quick centralized decisions, undermining the democratic ideal that masses can deliberate and decide; historical democracies have tended toward policies minimizing foreign entanglement for this reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic distrust of foreign trade/manufacture and preference for self-sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Because external contacts enlarge the unseen environment, democratic tendencies favor limiting foreign trade, manufacturing, and entanglement — seeking self-sufficiency to preserve a manageable political sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann links this to slogans like Self-Government and Independence, and to historical policies (e.g., Monroe Doctrine) intended to create a 'glacis' of republican states; when foreign connections are necessary, democrats seek protectionist or isolationist measures to simplify decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances to neutralize local and class interests
rubrics_metrics.description: In a large polity where common information and consent cannot be assumed, institutional design (checks and balances, separation of powers) is necessary to balance and deadlock local and class interests so a national government can act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann explains the Federalists' approach: they did not believe local assemblies would harmonize nationally, so they devised mechanisms (ambition counteracting ambition) to enable the government to 'control the governed' and to 'oblige it to control itself.' This institutional remedy substitutes magistracy for naked force and curbs parochial prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of elite attachments (force, patronage, privilege) to secure national governance
rubrics_metrics.description: To build an effective national government, leaders may need to enlist and bind elite interests (gentry, public creditors, manufacturers, shippers) through policies and fiscal measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann highlights Hamilton's strategy of attaching provincial notables to the Union via fiscal measures — an explicit use of patronage and privilege to secure cooperation and stabilize government in the absence of common democratic information or consent.
